doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Herman Chittison: pianist friend and patient
summary: Budd tells of hearing Chittison on radio, befriending him, and treating him for the lung problem that killed him; the block then begins the AMA insurance story.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Well how is music and medicine intertwined for you in your life?

Oh different ways. People — one small example of medicine and music would be Herman Chittison, the piano player, happens to be about my age. I had heard him many years ago when he was a Blue Note pianist on a program called the — some kind of photography — Flash Casey, Crime Photographer. It was from the radio, on Thursday nights. And the setting was in a place called the Blue Note. And every week it was a whodunnit thing. It was kind of interesting. But in the background music was this guy playing the piano. And I didn’t know who it was, but he became more popular than the program of people wondering who he is. It turned out it was Herman Chittison and he became known as the “Blue Note Pianist.” And I heard about that and I enjoyed his playing. I had a chance to meet him one time, many years later, about 1960 at a medical meeting and he was playing in the restaurant. And I went with another doctor friend because I wanted to hear him play and see him. I listened to him and talked to him and we became friends, and later he came to Cleveland and worked in a Stoeffer’s Restaurant there, and I went down to see him and all that. And he happened to come to me as a patient one time. He says “you are a doctor and I enjoyed talking to you and I have some © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -2-

indigestion and I’d like to see you about it.” I had a GI X-ray series and incidentally a chest X-ray, which was sort of routine in those days to make sure your chest, you didn’t have tuberculosis at least. And the radiologist said “this little thing in this lung there that looks bad to me if it was never there before it’s new and it’s dangerous. If it’s been there before it may be a calcified lymph node and don’t worry about it, see if you can get an old film.” So we got one from Akron, six months before, and it wasn’t seen then, so it’s new. And he said it doesn’t sound good. It’s in the middle of the lung and you can’t do a bronchoscopic examination, you have to do an exploratory in there. And Herman didn’t like that and he put it off. And we talked a lot. He’d come to my house and he would play the piano and we’d talk about music and he’d show me chords and so forth. And we’d get back to saying Herman it’s time to go and see the doctor. He finally, after about three months, he said “I think I’d better go and get that done, where shall I go?” And I said “go up to the University Hospital in Cleveland, they’re experts there and the Cleveland Clinic is very famous, you’ll find great people there.” He said “where do you go?” And I told him Deaconess Hospital. And he said “is there anybody there that does this kind of work well?” And I said “yes I know a young man who was in the Army and trained after the war with the clinic people, and he’s the head of our staff and he’s pretty good and he’s young and he’s a good friend.” So he said “well I’ll go to him.” And he went and had a lobectomy — part of one of his lungs removed — and the doctor said “this is only palliative, it’s not curative because it’s beyond where I can...” But Herman went back to work and played about a year. He finally got sick and got very short of breath. He came to see me, went to the hospital and in another day or so was dead. But that’s medicine and that sort of thing. And medicine-baseball: one time in my job as a doctor, the AMA and the House of Delegates, they wanted an insurance program for some of the doctors. There was a program at that time for disability for doctors or employees of doctors, and if you’re disabled well you get your benefits. But it was a generous one because you have to be so disabled that you can’t do your ordinary job, what you ordinarily do. And it turns out some doctors say “I’m seventy years old, I’m no longer able to do surgery I don’t think, but I can still practice medicine but I can’t do surgery, so I should have my disability.” And they argued about that, and the insurance policy exactly said you’ve got to be paid. So they almost went broke until that program ran out and then they looked for somebody else to give them coverage, and they got that Charlie Findlay who ran an insurance company, and he began going around to telephone the doctors in Michigan, in New Jersey, in Texas, in California, Ohio — the larger states where they had a lot of doctors to find somebody in that state that was fairly well known that might exert some influence to persuade the AMA perhaps to buy his particular policy.
